paras: The threatened lynching of Tom Fifer took place near Brewton, Alabama, in August 1903, after Fifer, a young Black farm hand, was accused of poisoning the water of the farmer who employed him and striking the farmer with a rock. Threats of lynching were reported while a sheriff's posse hunted him, but he was arrested the next day and jailed at Brewton under guard.

Matthew Crossley was described as a "prosperous farmer" living seven miles southwest of Brewton. According to the Montgomery Advertiser, Fifer was about 20 years old and had worked for Crossley for several months.

Early on the morning of August 24, Fifer was accused of dosing the family's water bucket with strychnine, and Crossley's daughter, the first to drink, was taken violently ill. The Advertiser's correspondent wrote that Fifer then claimed a mule was sick, struck Crossley with a rock when he went to the lot, wounding him on the head and breast, and escaped over a fence. Physicians expected all of those affected to recover.

Sheriff Raley and a posse pursued Fifer through the day, while the reports spoke of "Great indignation" and "threats of lynching." The Advertiser added that if the people of Crossley's neighborhood caught him before the sheriff jailed him, "he will be summarily dealt with."

On the afternoon of August 25, Sheriff James W. Raley and his posse took the accused from a south-bound freight flagged at the Tensaw River railroad bridge, about fourteen miles from Mobile. He was brought to Brewton that night and jailed, and the paper reported that because "Feeling runs high" in Crossley's neighborhood a strong guard would be placed around the jail. The surviving text of that report breaks off there, and no later report of an indictment, trial or attack on the jail was found.

Every report traced to the Montgomery Advertiser's Brewton correspondent, whose specials ran under the headlines "DASTARDLY ATTEMPT" and "ALLEGED POISONER CAUGHT." The Advertiser called the act "diabolical," said the accused had been "positively identified," and reported the neighbors' intention to deal with him summarily without comment. A shorter version ran in the Birmingham Age-Herald on August 25 and, a week later, in the Atlanta Constitution.
The story appeared only in white papers; no Black-press coverage of the case was found.
The first reports named the accused Tom Fifer, while the Advertiser's arrest report called him "Lee Pfeiffer"; the details of the crime and wounds are the same in both.

reader.title: Threatened lynching of Tom Fifer
bases: The papers report threats of lynching against a Black man accused of poisoning and assaulting a farmer's family, with no killing or attack reported (A1, A2, A3).

The coverage reports only threats that neighbors would deal 'summarily' with the accused, who was then arrested by the sheriff and jailed under guard; no killing is reported (A2, A3). The threatened act would have been extralegal punishment for an alleged crime, but the threateners are not counted or described (A1, A2).
All four reports trace to the Montgomery Advertiser's Brewton correspondent: A2 and A3 are its specials, A1 says it is 'A special to the Advertiser', and A4 repeats A1's text (A1, A2, A3, A4).

accounts.label: Montgomery Advertiser's Brewton correspondent
accounts.gist: The accused poisoned the water bucket intending to kill the whole family, then struck Crossley with a rock and fled; neighbors would deal with him summarily if they caught him first, and after his arrest feeling ran high.

accounts.label: Wire summary of the Advertiser special
accounts.gist: A shorter version naming Tom Fifer, reporting 'Great indignation' and 'threats of lynching'.

framing.detail: The Advertiser headlined 'DASTARDLY ATTEMPT' and 'ALLEGED POISONER CAUGHT', called the act 'diabolical', and reported the neighbors' intent to deal 'summarily' with the accused without criticism.
The Age-Herald and the Atlanta Constitution ran the short version under 'ATTEMPT TO POISON FAMILY' and 'Negro Put Poison in Water Bucket'.

conflicts.note: Same paper and correspondent, same case (Crossley poisoning, same wounds); the name likely differs by spelling or report. The later report (A3) followed the arrest.
'Crossby' appears only in the A1 subhead; its body text reads Crossley.
